Personas Are Not People: Identity as State, Not Attribute

Tamunotonye Harry Affiliation: University of Vermont, Department of Computer Science, Burlington, Vermont, USA and Yuanyuan Feng Affiliation: University of Vermont, Department of Computer Science, Burlington, Vermont, USA
Abstract.

Synthetic populations, large sets of simulated people, are increasingly used in place of real people to pretest surveys, simulate users and communities, and evaluate AI systems. Each simulated person is defined by a persona, a written profile of fixed traits, demographics, and attitudes that a language model is instructed to act out. Every such system assumes that a person’s identity is a stable attribute that behaves the same way in every situation the simulation presents. We show that this assumption is not a harmless simplification. Three decades of personality research find the opposite. How a given person behaves varies more across contexts than people vary from one another. Drawing on identity economics, which describes how different situations activate different identities and norms within the same person, we separate behavior into three parts, which are stable traits, the identity a context calls up, and the situation itself. We then prove, under two stated assumptions, that any simulation built on fixed personas, no matter how detailed the personas or how large the underlying model, cannot reproduce the part of a population’s behavior that is specific to it and its circumstances. We propose a new evaluation criterion based on this result and a person-in-context design that can meet it in principle. We test one version on a naturalistic Reddit personality corpus and on a published clinical-trial recruitment survey of a community with documented distrust of medical institutions. The design does produce context-dependent behavior when tested directly, but in neither setting does it fully match the real population, and we show where it falls short. The consequence for practice is a risk that synthetic-population evaluations misrepresent the groups whose behavior is most shaped by context, a distortion that richer personas cannot correct.

Keywords: 
synthetic populations, LLM personas, AI evaluation, within-person variance, context-dependent behavior, identity, representational harm, personality psychology, simulation of human behavior

1. Introduction

Companies and researchers now pretest surveys, products, and messages on AI-simulated populations before asking real customers or citizens, and some propose using the simulations instead of asking at all (Argyle et al., 2023; Bisbee et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026b). Some systems already hold billions of simulated people (Li et al., 2026b), built in part from hundreds of hours of real interviews (Park et al., 2024). These systems share one design choice. Each simulated person is a persona, a written profile, vector, or interview transcript that is prepared before the simulation runs. Some systems retrieve different parts of it for different questions, but what is stored about the person never changes. A persona therefore fixes the person’s identity too, which we take from Akerlof and Kranton (Akerlof and Kranton, 2000) to mean a person’s sense of self as a member of a social category, along with the norms for how members of that category act. A real person holds several identities, such as employee, parent, or friend, and which one is active depends on the situation, so the same person may be formal and careful in a meeting with colleagues and relaxed and joking at dinner with friends (§3.1). Current persona designs cannot represent this shift. Any change in behavior across situations is the large language model (LLM) improvising, and the persona itself never changes (Figure 1).

In personality psychology, most of the variation in trait-related behavior is within persons rather than between them (Fleeson and Gallagher, 2009; Fleeson, 2001). Identity economics (Akerlof and Kranton, 2000; Akerlof and Kranton, 2010) offers an account of this variation. A person belongs to several social categories, each category carries norms for how its members act, and the situation determines which category is active and therefore which norms the person follows (§2.2). Recent work has started to notice the symptoms. Studies report that fixed personas collapse toward a typical default (Ozkan, 2026) and compress variation within demographic groups (Wang et al., 2026), while other work lets the personality of a single dialogue agent shift as a conversation unfolds (Pielage et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2026). To our knowledge, none of this work says what a simulated population must reproduce to behave like a real one, and none represents identity as a state that context activates (§2). Existing validation does not fill that gap either. Persona adherence (Li et al., 2026b) asks whether a simulated person acts as its profile says. Test-retest consistency and prediction of held-out survey answers (Park et al., 2024) are internal-validity checks that ask whether a simulation reproduces what a person answered on the same kind of survey. Subgroup coverage (Batzner et al., 2025) asks whether the right kinds of people are included. None of these asks the external-validity question of whether simulated people behave like real people once the situation changes. We call a test of that question a behavioral-fidelity evaluation (do simulated people respond to a new situation the way real people do?).

The gap has consequences. Suppose a city emergency office pretests the wording of a flood evacuation alert on simulated residents, because a live test is impossible. A real resident may ignore a text from the city as one more automated message, yet leave at once when a neighbor knocks on the door or a relative calls. A persona that says “distrusts authorities” predicts that no version of the alert works, and a persona that leaves distrust out predicts that every version works. Either way, the office chooses its wording and its messenger on the model’s guess, and the residents who most need to leave may stay. The error matters more when the simulated people stand in for patients or citizens and the decision reaches a real community (§6.3).

We make three contributions.

  1. (1)

    Can richer personas fix this? No, and we give a formal proof. Any simulation built on a fixed persona cannot reproduce what is specific to a person beyond their group’s typical response, however detailed the persona and however large the model. The proof relies on two stated assumptions, and we test how it degrades when they only roughly hold (§4.2, Appendix B).

  2. (2)

    How would we know? A new evaluation criterion. Latent State-Trait (LST) fingerprint recovery has three parts. It asks how much of the variation in behavior is between people, how much comes from particular people in particular situations, and whether a simulation tracks each person’s specific response. The proof shows that, in principle, fixed personas cannot meet the third check (§4).

  3. (3)

    What would work? A person-in-context design and two tests of it. We build a person-in-context approach, in which a situation selects an identity state that the language model then acts out, and we test it against fixed personas on two real datasets. Fixed personas make each person behave almost the same in every situation, far more than real people do, and our design comes closer on all five personality traits we tested. On a published clinical-trial recruitment study, our design reproduces the overall effect of trust on how respondents rate the ads, and its behavior changes as expected when the identity state is switched. It does not reproduce the study’s central finding that which ad theme works best depends on how much a person trusts the healthcare system, and we explain why in §5. Person-specific signal is near zero for every system we test, so that test cannot yet separate them.

In principle, a person-in-context design can represent person-specific response to context, which a fixed persona provably cannot. In our tests, the implementation we built reproduces some features of the real data, such as the effect of trust, but not yet the finding that the best ad theme depends on trust. Closing that gap is an open problem.

2. Related Work

Our contribution connects three bodies of work that have not been brought together, namely synthetic populations for AI evaluation, behavioral science on how people act in context, and the critique of representational harm in generative systems.

2.1. Synthetic populations for AI evaluation

Simulated people are used for LLM-based evaluation in many ways, for example to pretest survey questions, to simulate public opinion, and to stress-test chat systems with simulated users. These systems fall into three families, which differ in how they represent identity.

The fixed-persona family dominates current systems. A persona, whether a categorical vector, a written profile, or an interview transcript, is set up in advance and does not change with the situation. MatrAIx (Li et al., 2026b) is the current large-scale example, with 8.3 billion persona records, a 1,290-dimension schema, and a 91.5% persona-adherence rate. Park et al. (Park et al., 2024) use two-hour interview transcripts as personas for 1,052 people, and report that, on held-out General Social Survey items, interview-based agents reach 83% of participants’ own test-retest consistency. Argyle et al. (Argyle et al., 2023) condition on demographics with lighter personas. Bisbee et al. (Bisbee et al., 2024) find that such synthetic survey responses have much less variance than real respondents, and that many regression coefficients differ significantly from human data. In this family, context stays outside the persona, and the language model alone supplies any adaptation.

The memory-evolving family adds accumulated experience to a fixed persona. Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023), SOTOPIA (Zhou et al., 2024), Concordia (Vezhnevets et al., 2023), OASIS (Yang et al., 2024), and AgentSociety (Piao et al., 2025) give agents a memory stream with reflection or planning. Variation then follows what has happened to the agent, closer to a diary than to identities that the present situation brings out.

The person-in-context family treats identity as a state that context activates. It has theoretical roots in self-categorization theory and multiple-self-aspects frameworks (McConnell, 2011), and related computational work exists for single dialogue agents. Pielage et al. (Pielage et al., 2026) model an assistant’s personality as latent states in a state machine whose transitions follow the conversation. Wei et al. (Wei et al., 2026) steer persona-related neurons in a model according to the situation. Lee et al. (Lee et al., 2025) build a persona from social identity, personal identity, and life context. These works adapt one agent within an interaction or enrich a single persona. We found none that represents a population of people with context-activated identities and tests it against real within-person variation. That is the gap we address.

Concurrent critiques. Several recent studies conclude from different angles that fixed personas are the wrong unit for population simulation. They report collapse toward a typical default in some scenarios (Ozkan, 2026), declining observer-rated persona expression over long conversations (Gonnermann-Müller et al., 2026), subgroup-specific distortions from multi-attribute personas (Taday Morocho et al., 2026), inconsistent subgroup alignment from sociodemographic prompting (Sun et al., 2025), and compressed variation within demographic groups, for which a longitudinal memory remedy is proposed (Wang et al., 2026). None derives an evaluation criterion from within-person variance or proposes a context-activated identity design.

2.2. Behavioral science on person-in-context

In personality research, most of the variation in trait-related behavior is within persons, from one moment to the next (Fleeson and Gallagher, 2009). This helped resolve the person-situation debate of the 1990s (Fleeson, 2001; Fleeson and Jayawickreme, 2015). Latent State-Trait (LST) theory (Steyer et al., 1992; Steyer et al., 2015) splits behavior into trait, state, and error, and variance ratios akin to intraclass correlations give each part’s share. Whole Trait Theory, which came later, describes a trait as a distribution of states around a stable level (Fleeson, 2001; Fleeson and Jayawickreme, 2015). Inspired by both, we write behavior as Y=τ+s⁡(X)+εY=\tau+s(X)+\varepsilon, a stable level plus a response to the situation plus noise. In §3.1 we extend s⁡(X)s(X) with a person-specific, context-activated term Ip,c,tI_{p,c,t}.

One study applies these methods to language-model behavior directly (Harry et al., 2026). In a Reddit corpus, it finds that most variance is within persons, about 72 to 74% across the 26 trait dimensions it measures, without removing measurement noise, in line with the psychological literature. It also finds that language models prompted with personas do not track context-driven change, which it calls state-blind. Han et al. (Han et al., 2026) also use Whole Trait Theory to read LLM agents and find that one personality prompt is expressed differently across four conversational settings.

Identity as a building block. Akerlof and Kranton (Akerlof and Kranton, 2000; Akerlof and Kranton, 2010) treat identity as a variable in a person’s decisions, with actions judged against the norms of the identity that is active. Trait Activation Theory (Tett and Guterman, 2000) reaches a compatible view, that situations activate traits through cues, and self-categorization theory (Turner et al., 1987) and the multiple-self-aspects framework (McConnell, 2011) agree. We found no synthetic-population system or evaluation built on any of them.

2.3. Representational harm in generative systems

Representational harm connects this work to questions of fairness and accountability. A synthetic population that flattens a group misrepresents that group, and decisions made from it reach real communities. Bender et al. (Bender et al., 2021) warn that scaling language models without attention to whose language is represented risks amplifying dominant viewpoints. Blodgett et al. (Blodgett et al., 2020) argue that work on “bias” often does not say which harms to which communities it addresses. Our criterion responds to this by naming one specific distortion, flattening of context-dependent behavior, and measuring it. Wang et al. (Wang et al., 2025) show that replacing human participants with LLMs can misportray and flatten identity groups. Two findings concern persona-based systems directly. Xiao et al. (Xiao et al., 2026) find that models with the highest per-persona fidelity produce the most polarized populations, so persona adherence and population fidelity can pull apart. Batzner et al. (Batzner et al., 2025) find that only 35% of 63 persona-based LLM studies report anything about representativeness. That is a separate problem, since a representative, transparently sampled set of personas is still fixed and would still fail our criterion. These critiques name the outcome but not its cause. We locate the flattening in one design choice, identity as a fixed attribute of the persona, which cannot match the real structure of within-person variation. Richer personas do not remove it.

2.4. Gap

Behavioral science models how people act in context, and identity economics accounts for the mechanism. Neither has been built into a synthetic-population system and tested there against real within-person variation, and current validation does not check for it. We add what the critique literature lacks (§2.1, §2.3), namely an explanation of why these failures occur, a new evaluation criterion derived from it (§4), and a formal result (§4.2) that, under two stated assumptions, the failure comes from the design, whatever the scale or prompting.

3. Framework: Person-in-Context Simulation

We split behavior into three parts, which are a stable attribute of the person, an identity state that the situation brings out, and the situation itself.

3.1. A Decomposition of Behavior

Let pp index persons, cc contexts, and tt the time point of an observation. A person can return to the same context at a different time point, for example the same subreddit a week later. In plain terms, behavior depends on who a person stably is, which identity the situation brings out, and what the situation demands. We write

Yp,c,t=f⁡(τp,Ip,c,t,Xc,t)+εp,c,t.Y_{p,c,t}=f(\tau_{p},I_{p,c,t},X_{c,t})+\varepsilon_{p,c,t}.
  • •

    τp\tau_{p} is the person’s stable attribute vector, made up of demographic attributes (such as age or income), habits, values, and dispositions that stay roughly the same across situations. Big Five inventories and values surveys measure the psychological part.

  • •

    Ip,c,tI_{p,c,t} is the identity state that the situation brings out. It is chosen from a set of possible identity states, each with its own norms for how a person in that state acts. Identity economics, Trait Activation Theory, self-categorization theory, and multiple-self-aspects frameworks motivate this (§2.2).

  • •

    Xc,tX_{c,t} is the situation, meaning the linguistic, social, and situational features of context cc at time tt.

  • •

    ff produces behavior from the three inputs. In the systems we study it is a large language model, and our results do not depend on how it works inside.

  • •

    εp,c,t\varepsilon_{p,c,t} is mean-zero noise specific to one time point, the part none of the other terms explain.

Applying the law of total variance twice, first conditioning on τp\tau_{p} and then on (Ip,c,t,Xc,t)(I_{p,c,t},X_{c,t}), splits the variance of YY into a between-person part, a within-person part driven by II and XX, and noise:

Var⁡(Y)=Varτ​[𝔼​(Y∣τ)]⏟between-person+𝔼τ​[Var​(f∣τ)]⏟within-person via ​I,X+Var⁡(ε).\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\underbrace{\mathrm{Var}_{\tau}[\mathbb{E}(Y\mid\tau)]}_{\text{between-person}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[\mathrm{Var}(f\mid\tau)]}_{\text{within-person via }I,X}+\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon).

Variation within a person can arise even without II. A fixed persona still behaves differently when Xc,tX_{c,t} changes, because ff responds to the situation directly. What requires Ip,c,tI_{p,c,t} is narrower, namely the part of within-person variation that is specific to the person. This is the interaction between who the person is and which situation they are in, which differs from the response to the situation that all persons share. Only when Ip,c,tI_{p,c,t} changes with context for a fixed person can this interaction be guaranteed to be person-specific. Otherwise it could be a side effect of how ff handles (τp,Xc,t)(\tau_{p},X_{c,t}). This is the property that the criterion in §4 detects. The decomposition has the standard form of multilevel models in personality psychology (Raudenbush and Bryk, 2002; Snijders and Bosker, 2011) and of Latent State-Trait theory (Steyer et al., 1992; Steyer et al., 2015). Our contribution is to use it as a specification for synthetic populations.

3.2. Kinds of Systems and Their Interface

A simulation system stores a representation of each person, builds a prompt for each situation, and calls a language model. The inputs that the model’s generation call receives are the system’s interface. A single-call system produces each response with one such call. A system with subroutines runs extra steps first, such as a rule or a second language-model call that scores which identity a situation brings out, and passes the result into the interface. The interface is then the full list of inputs to the generation call, whether they come from storage or from a subroutine. In the appendix, the generation function fLLMf_{\mathrm{LLM}} also carries independent sampling noise ηp,c\eta_{p,c} (random variation in the generated text, so the same input can give different responses on different calls), and the time index is dropped, since the propositions concern the person-context decomposition only.

We call each design a family and each implementation a system. The families differ in which inputs reach the model, whatever the number of calls.

  • •

    Fixed-persona family. The system stores one persona πp\pi_{p} that never changes, so the interface is (πp,Xc,t)(\pi_{p},X_{c,t}) and only the situation changes with context. Any identity-like adaptation comes from the language model’s own inference. MatrAIx (Li et al., 2026b), Park et al. (Park et al., 2024), and Argyle et al. (Argyle et al., 2023) are in this family.

  • •

    Memory-evolving family. The system stores a persona and a growing record of past interactions Mp,tM_{p,t}, so the interface is (πp,Mp,t,Xc,t)(\pi_{p},M_{p,t},X_{c,t}) (Park et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024; Vezhnevets et al., 2023; Piao et al., 2025). The record grows with time and is not indexed by context. The record encodes the agent’s history.

  • •

    Person-in-context family. The system stores a stable attribute vector τp\tau_{p} and a set ℐp\mathcal{I}_{p} of identity states available to the person. A subroutine πI\pi_{I} selects which state to activate, written Ip,c,t∼πI​(τp,Xc,t)I_{p,c,t}\sim\pi_{I}(\tau_{p},X_{c,t}). The interface is (τp,Ip,c,t,Xc,t)(\tau_{p},I_{p,c,t},X_{c,t}). The set is fixed for each person, and only the realized state changes with context. This is the design we propose, and we know of no production system that uses it.

Adding subroutines to a fixed-persona system does not change its family if every subroutine reads only πp\pi_{p} and Xc,tX_{c,t}. Its output is then still a function of (πp,Xc,t)(\pi_{p},X_{c,t}). What matters for the propositions is whether any interface input is both specific to the person and changes with context for that person. Only the person-in-context family has one.

Building ℐp\mathcal{I}_{p} from data (§5.2, §5.3) showed that the set can also include a baseline state, a default that a person returns to when no context is strong, like the center of a person’s state distribution in Whole Trait Theory. Whether the set has a baseline is an empirical question. The Chameleon set has one baseline and five activated states, and the motivational-themes set has no baseline and six activated states.

3.3. A Limit Built Into the Fixed-Persona Design

We do not claim that fixed-persona and memory-evolving systems fail at what they were built for. Sampling varied profiles for product testing (Li et al., 2026b), simulating social dynamics in a sandbox (Park et al., 2023), and predicting individual attitudes (Park et al., 2024) are legitimate goals, judged fairly by their own criteria. Our claim is narrower. These systems are now proposed for behavioral simulation, which means reproducing how a population responds across contexts. For that goal they meet a target their design does not represent.

In a fixed-persona system the persona does not change with context, so no input says which identity the situation has brought out for this person. The model must infer one from the persona and the situation, or a subroutine supplies one that reads only those two inputs. Either way the output is a function of (πp,Xc,t)(\pi_{p},X_{c,t}) alone (Proposition 1, §4.2), so person-context interaction is limited by the variance that the model’s own inference adds (Han et al., 2026; Harry et al., 2026). This holds for every fixed-persona system, whatever the persona format or the model. A richer persona adds between-person variance and does not create person-context interaction. A similar argument applies to memory-evolving systems, whose memory is a within-person state but is not indexed by identity options the person can activate. Their variation follows the sequence of past events, with no role for the norms of the present situation.

The person-in-context family can represent person-specific response to context by construction. Whether a given implementation reproduces real within-person variance is an empirical question, which the criterion in §4 answers. That the family is capable of it is a property of the design, whatever the implementation. The fixed-persona failures in §5.2 and §5.3 follow from this. The memory-evolving family is open to a similar argument, but neither dataset tests it, because both compare only fixed-persona arms (A and B) with the person-in-context arm (C). Arm C’s results concern one implementation (our specification of the identity states and how they are activated). They do not change what the design itself can represent (§6.1).

4. Evaluation Criterion: LST Fingerprint Recovery

§3 shows that only the person-in-context family can represent Ip,c,tI_{p,c,t} as person-specific. A new criterion turns that difference into something measurable, which we call Latent State-Trait (LST) fingerprint recovery. A fingerprint is a pattern specific enough to identify who it belongs to. A population’s LST fingerprint is how stable people are relative to one another, and how much and in what way each person varies across situations. The criterion, built on the LST variance decomposition (§3.1) (Steyer et al., 1992; Eid and Diener, 2004), checks whether a synthetic population reproduces the real fingerprint as well as the average response levels.

4.1. The Criterion

LST fingerprint recovery compares a synthetic system 𝒜\mathcal{A} with a real population on three components.

  1. (1)

    Between-person share (ICC). The intraclass correlation (ICC, bias-corrected) is the fraction of all variation in behavior that comes from stable differences between people. The rest is one person varying across situations, plus noise. A system that inflates this share treats identity as more fixed than real behavior supports.

  2. (2)

    Person-context interaction variance (VarP×C\mathrm{Var}_{P\times C}). This is the variance left after removing person and context main effects. It comes from particular people in particular contexts (§3.1). A system can match the real ICC and still show almost no interaction, because everyone reacts to context in the same way. ICC alone cannot tell these cases apart.

  3. (3)

    Person-specific signal (person-specific residual correlation). This is the component our proof addresses. A fixed persona cannot reach it by design, and a person-in-context system can in principle. Two people of the same general type, for example both skeptical of institutions, still react differently to a given situation. The shared, predictable part is state-typical. The leftover part is person-specific, the signature a system must capture if it claims to simulate that person, beyond their type.

    Formally, Rp,chuman=m⁡(λp,c)+Δp,cR^{\text{human}}_{p,c}=m(\lambda_{p},c)+\Delta_{p,c}. Here λp\lambda_{p} is person pp’s soft membership across the identity states in ℐp\mathcal{I}_{p} (§3.2; Appendix B), m⁡(λp,c)m(\lambda_{p},c) is the state-typical shift, and Δp,c\Delta_{p,c} is the person-specific residual. The third component is the correlation between the system’s residual Rp,c𝒜R^{\mathcal{A}}_{p,c} and Δp,c\Delta_{p,c} only, leaving out the state-typical part m⁡(λp,c)m(\lambda_{p},c). The reason is that a system could match the full human residual Rp,chumanR^{\text{human}}_{p,c} by copying state-typical patterns that a stated persona often reveals, without representing anything specific to the person.

A population that recovers all three, with real-scale ICC, real-scale interaction variance, and non-trivial person-specific signal, reproduces the target’s LST fingerprint. A fixed persona falls short on the third component by design, as §4.2 proves. Whether a given person-in-context implementation reaches it is an empirical question.

4.2. A Formal Limit for the Fixed-Persona Family

Under the two assumptions below, a fixed-persona system cannot meet the third component. This is a formal result about the design, so it does not depend on tuning or on any dataset. Full statements and proofs are in Appendix B.

Mediation (Proposition 1; proof in Appendix B). The interaction residual of a fixed-persona system has the form Rp,c𝒜=g⁡(πp,Xc)+ηp,cR^{\mathcal{A}}_{p,c}=g(\pi_{p},X_{c})+\eta_{p,c}, where η\eta is independent sampling noise and Cov⁡(g,η)=0\mathrm{Cov}(g,\eta)=0. It contains nothing beyond the persona, the context, and noise, however rich πp\pi_{p} is. This limits the correlation with the person-specific residual. It does not limit how elaborate or context-sensitive g⁡(πp,Xc)g(\pi_{p},X_{c}) can be. No persona can make that sensitivity track Δp,c\Delta_{p,c}, because πp\pi_{p} does not change with context and carries no information indexed by person and context.

Person-specific non-transmission (Proposition 2; proof in Appendix B). A fixed-persona system’s output cannot correlate with a real person’s specific signature, and any apparent match comes from matching general type. The Key Assumption says that whoever builds the persona has no information about Δp,c\Delta_{p,c} beyond the person’s identity state and demographics. The Context Exogeneity Assumption says that the context a person appears in also carries no such information. Under both, with the independence conditions in Appendix B, Cov⁡(Rp,c𝒜,Δp,c)=0\mathrm{Cov}(R^{\mathcal{A}}_{p,c},\Delta_{p,c})=0 exactly.

A robustness corollary relaxes both assumptions to approximate independence. If the persona leaks at most ϵ1\epsilon_{1} and the context assignment leaks at most ϵ2\epsilon_{2} of information about Δp,c\Delta_{p,c}, then

|Cov⁡(Rp,c𝒜,Δp,c)|≤4​M2​(ϵ1+ϵ2)/2.|\mathrm{Cov}(R^{\mathcal{A}}_{p,c},\Delta_{p,c})|\leq 4M^{2}\sqrt{(\epsilon_{1}+\epsilon_{2})/2}.

Here MM bounds the size of the residuals, which is finite because ratings lie on a fixed scale. The quantity ϵ1\epsilon_{1} measures how much knowing the persona tells you about Δp,c\Delta_{p,c}, beyond identity state and demographics, and ϵ2\epsilon_{2} measures the same for the context. Both are mutual information, and zero means no leak. The bound says a small leak allows only a small correlation, so the result degrades gradually and does not collapse. The Key Assumption is easier to defend for thin, schema-based personas than for rich ones, and the Context Exogeneity Assumption is easier to defend for experimentally assigned contexts than for observed ones.

What the proof adds beyond the definition. The result would be empty if it only restated that a persona holds no information about Δp,c\Delta_{p,c}. It says more. Proposition 1 shows that a fixed-persona output depends on the persona, the context, and noise only, for any language model and any persona, which rules out the common hope that richer personas or larger models will close the gap. The assumptions are not part of the definition, and they can fail, for example when a persona is built from a person’s own behavior across contexts. The corollary bounds the effect when they hold only approximately. The prediction can also be tested. If personas leaked person-specific information, Arm A’s correlation with the real residual would be large, and in §5.2 it is small (0.026).

What this establishes. No fixed-persona system that meets the two assumptions can reach the third component beyond a small margin set by the corollary, whatever the model scale or data. Richer prompts or larger models can improve the first two components without touching this limit.

4.3. Scope: What the Criterion Does Not Establish

The criterion has two limits. First, the proof concerns the third component only, so it does not say that fixed personas must show inflated ICC or near-zero interaction variance. Those are diagnostics that we report for every system in §5.2. A fixed-persona system could show real-scale ICC or substantial interaction variance and still fail the third component. Second, the result depends on the two assumptions, or their approximate version. They are claims about how personas are built and how contexts are assigned, and neither follows from context-invariance alone. A persona built from a demographic profile and a stated identity state meets the Key Assumption directly, because Δp,c\Delta_{p,c} is by construction what such instruments cannot see. A persona built by hand-picking a person’s own responses across contexts would break it, because the persona would then contain the signal that Proposition 2 assumes it lacks.

Within this scope, the criterion gives person-in-context systems a target that fixed-persona systems cannot meet in principle, and gives any implementation of πI\pi_{I} a concrete three-part measure. §5.2 and §5.3 apply it to two datasets.

5. Empirical Tests of the Criterion

The proof in §4.2 concerns what the fixed-persona design can represent. The experiments ask what the data show about fixed personas and what Arm C, a first, theory-motivated implementation of the alternative, achieves. In Chameleon, fixed personas (Arms A and B) place almost all variation between people, where real people show almost none, and in the motivational-themes study their agreement with the published pattern changes from 5 of 6 directions to 0 of 6 when one sentence is added. Arm C comes closest to the real variance structure on every Chameleon trait, it reproduces the effect of trust in the study, and its behavior follows the identity state it is given. Person-specific signal is near zero for every system we test, and Arm C does not yet reproduce the study’s interaction between ad theme and trust. We trace that gap to how the implementation represents trust, as a single level that does not change with context (§5.3.3), which is the flattening that §6.3 names as a risk.

We chose the two datasets for what each can test. Chameleon records three posts from each of 1,667 people in different subreddits. Its repeated measures within each person, scored on many trait dimensions in a naturalistic corpus, make it the direct test of the between-person share and of person-specific signal. The motivational-themes study is not a dataset in the usual sense. It is a published survey experiment with one rating set per person, and we use its reported coefficients, sample demographics, and survey wording as a target. Because the real effect is known, we can say precisely where a simulation departs from it. Where the difference does not matter, we call both of them datasets.

5.1. Experimental Setup

Each dataset uses the same three arms, which differ only in what the language model is told about the person. Arm A (fixed persona) states a trait of the person once, such as “skeptical of institutions”, whatever the context. Arm B (fixed persona plus context) states the same trait and adds a neutral mention of the context, which tests whether naming the situation is enough when the person does not change. Arm C (person-in-context) states no fixed trait. It computes an identity state for each (person, context) pair, and the model acts out that state. Arms A and B are fixed-persona systems and neither keeps a record of past interactions, so neither dataset tests the memory-evolving family (§3.3). Appendix Table 15 shows what the model receives in each arm, and Appendix D gives the prompt for each arm.

Arm C builds its identity states in two steps. First, we construct a set of candidate identity states for the population. For Chameleon we fit a Gaussian mixture model (GMM), a statistical method that finds groups of similar observations in data without predefined labels. In our case the observations are users’ trait scores, so the groups are users with similar trait profiles. For the motivational-themes study we write the states from clinical-recruitment literature, independently of the target study, and check them for circularity. Second, each person’s affinity for each state is matched against the context to pick one active state. Figures 3 and 4 in the appendix diagram the two pipelines. We fix each specification before testing it on real data. Any later revision is reported as a separate, documented version (Appendix C).

All arms use the same elicitation format, in which the model gives a short reasoning and then a rating (Appendix C.5), and the same model, Claude Haiku 4.5 at temperature 0.7. The model generates behavior in every arm. In Chameleon it also scores, in separate calls, how well each subreddit matches each identity state’s cues. In the motivational-themes study, the cue scores for the four ads are fixed numbers set in the code by the authors from the specification’s activation cues. We chose Claude Haiku 4.5 because its training data end in February 2025, before the motivational-themes study was published in March 2026, whereas later models may have been trained on its preprint and could recall the results.

The two datasets test different parts of the criterion. Chameleon tests the first component (between-person share) and the third, person-specific signal, directly. The motivational-themes study has one observation per person, so it cannot test the third component. We compare each arm with the published aggregate coefficients instead, which tests the second component, whether the system reproduces the real person-context interaction in aggregate.

5.2. A Naturalistic Check: Chameleon

This check asks whether each system reproduces a known pattern in real people, in which most of what varies in their behavior is within each person, from one situation to the next, and little is between people. The target is the Chameleon dataset (Harry et al., 2026), with 1,667 Reddit users and three posts each in different subreddits. Each post is scored on twenty-six trait dimensions, including the five Big Five personality traits (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and openness), which are the outcomes each simulation must reproduce. The other twenty-one dimensions, from values, self-determination, and risk-taking scales, describe the person in the persona. In the real data about 1% of the variation is between people, and almost all of it is within each person across situations (§2.2). This uses a bias-corrected ICC, which removes the noise that three posts per person add.

On the first component, fixed personas show the opposite of the real pattern (Table 1). The real between-person share is about 1% (mean ICC 0.013), and Arms A and B place it at 91% and 80%. Arm C is the closest to the real value on all five traits and on average (0.285), and it recovers extraversion almost exactly (0.023 against 0.019). On the other four traits it remains above the real value, by 24 to 65 times on agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness, and below it on neuroticism. On the third component, person-specific signal is near zero for every arm (mean correlation 0.026 for Arm A, 0.025 for Arm B, and 0.004 for Arm C), and only extraversion is significant for all three (Table 1). This is the pattern Proposition 2 predicts for fixed personas. Their small positive values are what the robustness corollary (§4.2) expects, since a persona built from scores of the user’s own posts, and subreddits that users chose for themselves, can carry a little information about that user’s specific responses. With about 4,570 comparisons per trait, the test can reliably detect a correlation of about 0.04 or more (80% power, Appendix C.1). It therefore rules out a correlation well above that size in every arm and cannot separate the arms below it, so whether the person-in-context design recovers person-specific signal remains open.

5.3. A Published Target: The Motivational-Themes Study

The motivational-themes study (Harry and others, 2026) asked which advertising themes make a clinical-trial recruitment ad effective for Black adults in the United States, measured by how appealing respondents found the ad and how willing they were to participate and to recommend the trial. It also measured each respondent’s trust in the healthcare system, because distrust of medical institutions is documented in this community (Scharff et al., 2010; Armstrong et al., 2013) and could change how a theme lands. We use its published results as the target.

5.3.1. Setting and Reproduction Target

The study surveyed 829 Black adults. Each saw one of four ad themes (contribution to science, community benefit, blood-pressure management, financial compensation), a between-subject design. They rated appeal, willingness to participate, and willingness to recommend on 5-point scales. The target has two parts. First, no theme has a significant main effect on any outcome (p=.25p=.25 to .93.93). Second, theme and trust interact for the blood-pressure theme. All six blood-pressure by trust odds ratios are below 1 at both trust extremes relative to neutral, which means lower odds of a favorable rating. Significance alternates by outcome between the trust side and the distrust side. The target is this six-coefficient directional pattern, which is stricter than significance at both extremes (Appendix Table 10 lists the published design and values). For each arm we estimate the same six interactions and compare their signs with the published ones. The main analysis is a linear model in rating points with the contribution-to-science theme and neutral trust as baselines, and Appendix Table 11 repeats the comparison under seven analysis specifications.

The theme main effect does not separate the families, but the interaction is informative, since it requires the same theme to evoke a different response depending on a person-level trait. A fixed persona can reproduce part of this pattern in aggregate, because the language model links a stated trait to the ad text on its own. It cannot represent an identity that changes with the theme. The aggregate interaction is therefore a coarse test of whether a system represents the shift, since it cannot show whether any single simulated person changed.

5.3.2. Materials and Cohort

All three arms see the study’s advertisement text and outcome wording word for word. Arm C uses six identity states written from the literature (Appendix C.3). The Medical Skeptic state, on which the target interaction depends, is driven mainly by trust tier (activation probability 0.70 for distrust, 0.35 for neutral, 0.15 for trust), with capped demographic modifiers that cannot outvote trust. Appendix C.3 gives the calibration history.

Assignment is between-subject, as in the original study. We use 6,632 demographically resampled personas, one theme each, and all three arms run on identical cells. As §5.1 explains, Claude Haiku 4.5’s training data end in February 2025, thirteen months before the study’s publication, which makes contamination unlikely.

5.3.3. Results

The generative step responds to the active state. In the full run, 479 of 6,632 personas received, by chance, at least one response under an active Medical Skeptic state and one under their theme’s own state. The paired within-person difference is large and consistent (−1.76-1.76 appeal, −1.24-1.24 participate, −2.44-2.44 recommend), with the same direction in 87 to 100% of personas (Appendix Figure 5). A forced, matched 30-per-condition check gives non-overlapping 95% intervals. Switching a persona’s active state reliably changes behavior in the expected direction.

At n=6,632n=6{,}632, Arm C reproduces the trust main effect but not the interaction. An initial n=829n=829 run, matching the original study, was ambiguous. Interaction effects need larger samples than main effects to detect, so the cohort grew to n=6,632n=6{,}632, with roughly 500 to 630 personas per critical cell. At this size Arm C shows a large, precise trust main effect. Mean appeal rises from 2.41 (distrust) to 3.04 (neutral) to 3.42 (trust), tracking the activation rate of the Medical Skeptic state (0.78, 0.43, 0.22; cell means in Appendix Table 13). For the six blood-pressure by trust coefficients, we compare the direction of each simulated interaction with the published one (Appendix Table 11, row 2). Arm C matches 2 of 6, and both matches are coefficients close to zero. Arm A matches 5 of 6. Arm B, which adds only a theme sentence to Arm A, matches 0 of 6. Two arms that differ by one sentence give opposite directions, so a fixed persona’s agreement with the published direction reflects incidental wording, so it is weak evidence that the persona represents the mechanism. Guessing would match 3 of 6 on average, so a count is a coarse test. The larger sample ruled out under-sampling as the explanation, and did not produce the interaction.

The diagnosis concerns structure. The Medical Skeptic state’s activation floor is the same for all four themes by design. It can shift the level of activation by theme, but not the slope of the response to trust. Only a theme-dependent slope can produce an interaction. Without one, the model yields a general main effect, and this limit holds at any sample size. Arm C also rates the blood-pressure theme lower than the contribution-to-science theme at every trust level (mean appeal 2.78 against 3.16 at neutral trust; Appendix Table 13), a theme main effect the real study did not find. For Arm A the limit comes from the design (Propositions 1 and 2). For Arm C it is a gap in this particular πI\pi_{I}, and the natural-experiment check shows the mechanism itself is not barred from closing it (Appendix Table 3 summarizes both datasets).

A theory-motivated refinement does not close the gap. Amplifying the trust-linked state’s activation spread for the blood-pressure theme (fixed before evaluation, Appendix C.3) does not raise the match count under the contribution-to-science baseline (1 of 6, against 2 for the domain-general mechanism). With a pooled-theme baseline it reaches 3 of 6, and Arm A falls to 2 or 3, so the order of these arms depends on the baseline. We make no claim that the refinement improves on the domain-general mechanism, and because the amplified theme was chosen knowing where the real effect lies, it is also a weaker test. The more useful result is the shape of the real effect. All six published coefficients are negative. High-trust and high-distrust respondents both rate the blood-pressure theme lower than neutral-trust respondents. A mechanism that moves along one trust axis cannot produce a dip at both extremes (Figure 2).

5.4. Interpretation: What Both Datasets Show

Neither dataset tests whether the person-in-context family is capable of context-dependent behavior, since the natural-experiment and forced-contrast checks in §5.3.3 show that it is. They test whether this implementation of πI\pi_{I} closes the gap in practice, which Proposition 2 does not address.

The failure can be diagnosed. The real effect dips at both trust extremes, a shape that no single-axis mechanism can represent (Figure 2), which is why the theme-amplified refinement produces no gain in Appendix Table 11. Chameleon adds a complementary view. Its real within-person signal is faint, so it tests whether the implementation’s gain in aggregate variance carries over to person-specific signal, and so far it does not (§5.2). Appendix Table 3 sets the two datasets side by side. Together they show what the implementation already does, which is to produce behavior that follows the active state, and where work remains, in the choice of state and its link to person-specific signal.

6. Discussion

6.1. What the empirical tests show, and what they do not

The proof and the implementation are separate questions. Propositions 1 and 2 (§4) concern the design, and the experiments concern one implementation of the alternative. The difficulty in those tests concentrates in πI\pi_{I}, the step that selects the identity state, while the generative step, ff, performs well (§5.4).

Some of what we observe comes from the language model as well as from the design. Ratings follow a stated trait almost mechanically, and Arm A’s appeal ratings sit close to 2, 3, and 4 for distrust, neutral, and trust in every theme (Appendix C.4). One added sentence reversed five of the six interaction coefficients (Arm B). And the model responds strongly and in the expected direction when its active identity state is switched (§5.3.3), so the weak point is choosing the state. Acting it out works. The theory does not supply these facts about language models as simulators, and they should be rechecked with other models.

6.2. What this changes for evaluation practice

Persona adherence is the right check for the tasks that fixed-persona and memory-evolving systems were built for, namely covering varied profiles (Li et al., 2026b), predicting individual attitudes (Park et al., 2024), and simulating sandbox dynamics (Park et al., 2023). It is the wrong check when such systems are proposed for behavioral simulation, because §3.3 shows that a design can satisfy persona adherence and still be unable to produce the person-context interaction that behavioral simulation needs. Any claim of behavioral simulation should report the criterion in §4 directly instead of inferring it from adherence or demographic accuracy.

The motivational-themes study adds guidance for the one family that can simulate behavior in principle. Because the failure sits in πI\pi_{I}, auditing the generative step alone checks necessary behavior but not sufficient behavior, so evaluations should also audit πI\pi_{I} against real population data (Appendix C.3) and should not treat a literature-grounded specification as self-validating.

6.3. What this changes for identity representation

The fixed-persona design misrepresents groups whose behavior depends on context, and richer personas do not remove the problem. The distrust example from the introduction applies here, since a fixed persona stores distrust as a static attribute or leaves it out, and neither represents a state that the situation activates, as with distrust of medical institutions in the motivational-themes study (Scharff et al., 2010; Armstrong et al., 2013). §5.3.3 shows the risk is concrete, because our own person-in-context design, built to represent trust as context-dependent, produces a version of the same flattening. The risk therefore appears whenever a mechanism that selects identity states under-represents how a trait depends on context.

This also moves an accountability question without removing it. A fixed persona’s content can be traced to a stated source, such as demographic conditioning or a profile instrument. A person-in-context system also needs someone to specify ℐp\mathcal{I}_{p} itself (the set of identity states available to each person, §3.2), meaning which identity states exist, what activates them, and whether a behavior counts as state-typical or person-specific. That choice is an interpretation. Our own mechanism needed four locked revisions (documented versions, each fixed in writing before it was run and each prompted by a failed internal check) before it passed those checks, and the first three versions, though literature-grounded, failed them. The question shifts from what the persona says to who decides what a person’s possible identity states are.

6.4. Limitations

Data. The 6,632 simulated personas in the motivational-themes study match the published share of each demographic group, such as age or income, but not how those characteristics combine in real respondents. The Chameleon test uses the real users, with three posts each (§5.2). Method. The identity states are written by hand, so the results concern this implementation and say nothing about learned mechanisms (§6.5). In Chameleon, Claude Haiku 4.5 also scores how well each subreddit matches each identity state (Appendix C), in a separate call from the one that generates behavior, so shared biases may carry through, a concern raised for LLM-as-judge setups (Li et al., 2026a), and we did not test for this. In the motivational-themes study the cue scores were set by the authors, and the Medical Skeptic score was revised after a pilot (Appendix C.3). The three identity-state panels were isolated agent sessions of Claude Sonnet 5.5, one model family with no human raters. Their agreement rules out one unlucky sample, but not a bias that all three share. Scope. The framework models cross-sectional response only, and the between-subject motivational-themes study limits that test to the aggregate interaction. The proof does not depend on any of these.

6.5. Forward

Three directions follow. First, §5.3.3 motivates activation mechanisms that do not move along a single trust axis, since the real effect dips at both trust extremes. One outcome can arise from different states, for example institutional distrust at one extreme and a different skepticism at the other. Second, it is open whether the baseline-plus-activated-states structure in §3.2 is general or specific to Chameleon. A related test is whether Arm C does best on the trait whose context cues are clearest, which could explain why it recovers extraversion (§5.2). We have not tested this. Third, because the difficulty sits in πI\pi_{I}, it could be learned against held-out real data instead of set by hand (Wu et al., 2026), for example with an input-driven switching state-space model in which context drives transitions between identity states and a language model writes the behavior from the current state. Testing it needs longitudinal data that our datasets lack.

Ethical Considerations

Data and human subjects. We collected no new human-subjects data, and both datasets are already published. Chameleon is a public dataset of pseudonymous trait scores computed from public Reddit posts. It keeps the original post identifiers, so a record could in principle be linked to a public post. We made no attempt to identify, link, or contact any user, and we report results only in aggregate. The motivational-themes study contributes its published coefficients, sample demographics, and survey wording (Harry and others, 2026). We used the advertisement text only as a fixed input to language models, and did not use it to recruit or contact anyone. An institutional review board determined through its self-determination process that the project is not human-subjects research.

Population construction and the risk of encoding stereotypes. The identity-state specification in §5.3 was built for a population, Black adults evaluating clinical-trial recruitment materials, for whom misrepresentation has real stakes, given the documented history of harm and eroded trust around clinical research (Scharff et al., 2010; Alsan and Wanamaker, 2018). Three steps address this. The state content and demographic modifiers came from the independent health-behavior and clinical-recruitment literature, without using the target study’s results (Appendix C.3). Three isolated, blind sessions of Claude Sonnet 5.5 checked the specification without access to the target study’s findings (three sessions of one model, which are not independent raters; see §6.4). And the paper’s central claim is that institutional distrust in this population is context-activated, so assigning a static “distrusts the healthcare system” trait to a demographic group is the essentializing move the paper argues against. This does not remove the risk of misuse, because a published state specification could be separated from its context-activation framing.

Deployment risk. This work does not support replacing engagement with underrepresented populations by simulation, and our results are evidence against doing so. A reader could conclude that a validated person-in-context system could substitute for focus groups, surveys, or community engagement, especially for populations that are costly to recruit. That is where substitution would do the most harm. Our mechanism was literature-grounded, checked by blind model sessions, and run on a sample eight times the size of the original study, and it still did not reproduce the published interaction. This weakens the case for treating current synthetic output as a substitute for the represented population. These methods suit stress-testing evaluation infrastructure, but decisions about real populations need independent validation.

Reproducibility. We document the specifications, the main calibration decisions, and the fixed parameters behind each result (Appendices C.1, C.2, and C.3). Code, data, and saved model outputs are at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/state-persona-eval/.

Generative AI usage statement. Generative AI tools were used for editing assistance and for re-running analyses to check reported numbers against the raw output of each experiment. The authors designed the study, ran the experiments, and take full responsibility for the content of this paper, including the accuracy of all claims, numbers, and citations. Language models are also the subject of the study, as the systems under evaluation.
